s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Appearance as an Outward Manifestation of Form
s.d: appearance as the form of that which is seen
s.c: In some languages a strictly literal translation of ⟦Matthew 28:3|Matthew 28:3⟧ might be misinterpreted to mean that there was something jagged about the outline of Jesus’ appearance. The focus, of course, is upon the brightness, and therefore it may be important to translate ‘his appearance was bright like lightning.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: to observe something with continuity and attention, often with the implication that what is observed is something unusual
s.g: to observe; to be a spectator of; to look at

s.dp: Association › Visit
s.d: to go to see a person on the basis of friendship and with helpful intent
s.g: to visit; to go to see

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Shame, Disgrace, Humiliation
s.d: to cause someone to be publicly exhibited as an object of shame or disgrace

s.dp: Constructions › Open Constructions
s.d: a rather large, normally semicircular open structure capable of seating several thousand people and often used for public assemblies
s.c: The emphasis in ⟦Acts 19:29|Acts 19:29⟧ is upon the theater as a place for assembly and not as a place for dramas. In some languages the most appropriate equivalent is actually ‘meeting place.’ In other instances one may use a term which designates an ‘enclosure.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: (derivative of {L:θεωρέω<SDBG:θεωρέω:000000>}[a] ‘to observe,’ {D:24.14}) an unusual object or event which is observed

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: a chemical found in pale yellow mineral form; burns readily in air and is found in regions of vulcanic activity such as the Dead Sea area; causes land to be infertile; associated with punishment from God
s.c: In the NT θεῖον is always associated in some way with fire and refers to the kinds of burning hot rocks involved in volcanic eruptions. The closest equivalent in a number of languages is ‘burning stones’ or ‘fiery hot stones’ or ‘fiery red stones.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: pertaining to having the nature of God

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (derivative of {L:θεός<SDBG:θεός:000000>}[a] ‘God,’ {D:12.1}) the nature or state of being God
s.c: The expression ‘divine nature’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘just what God is like’ or ‘how God is’ or ‘what God is.’ In ⟦Romans 1:20|Romans 1:20⟧ ‘deity’ may sometimes be expressed as ‘the fact that he is God’ or ‘… is truly God.’|In ⟦2 Peter 1:4|2 Peter 1:4⟧ ‘to share in the very being of God,’ one may speak of ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to become in a measure like God.’ It is important, of course, to avoid the implication that people can become completely God.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (derivative of {L:θεός<SDBG:θεός:000000>}[a] ‘God,’ {D:12.1}) the nature or state of being God
s.c: The expression ‘divine nature’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘just what God is like’ or ‘how God is’ or ‘what God is.’ In ⟦Romans 1:20|Romans 1:20⟧ ‘deity’ may sometimes be expressed as ‘the fact that he is God’ or ‘… is truly God.’|In ⟦2 Peter 1:4|2 Peter 1:4⟧ ‘to share in the very being of God,’ one may speak of ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to become in a measure like God.’ It is important, of course, to avoid the implication that people can become completely God.

s.dp: Features of Objects › Color
s.d: sulfureous yellow, yellow as sulfur
s.c: Note that in ⟦Revelation 9:17|Revelation 9:17⟧ the three colors parallel three plagues, fire, smoke, and sulfur, and it may therefore be useful to translate the latter part of ⟦Revelation 9:17|Revelation 9:17⟧ as ‘they had breastplates red as fire, blue as sapphire, and yellow as sulfur.’ See also LN 79.37.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: (derivative of {L:θέλω<SDBG:θέλω:000002>}[c] ‘to desire,’ {D:25.1}) that which is desired or wished for

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: (derivative of {L:θέλω<SDBG:θέλω:000000>}[a] ‘to purpose,’ {D:30.58}) that which is purposed, intended, or willed

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire Strongly
s.d: (an idiom, literally: desire of the flesh) desire for sexual gratification

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: to desire to have or experience something
s.g: to desire; to want; to wish
s.c: As may be noted, in translating θέλησις, θέλημα (LN 25.2), βούλημα (LN 25.4), and εὐδοκία (LN 25.8), there is a tendency to employ verbs rather than nouns. This is true especially in languages outside the Indo-European family of languages. Wanting, desiring, and wishing are essentially psychological events or states and accordingly are most frequently expressed in languages by verbs.

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: to purpose, generally based upon a preference and desire
s.c: It is also possible that θέλω in ⟦Colossians 1:27|Colossians 1:27⟧ focuses more upon ‘desire’ (see LN 25.1).

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View
s.d: to have a particular view or opinion about something
s.g: to be of an opinion; to think something is so
s.c: Since θέλω in ⟦2 Peter 3:5|2 Peter 3:5⟧ is the only NT occurrence with this meaning, a number of scholars prefer to interpret θέλω in this context as referring to intention or evident purpose, in which case the meaning would be related to θέλω (LN 30.58).

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: to desire to have or experience something
s.g: to desire; to want; to wish
s.c: As may be noted, in translating θέλησις (LN 25.2), βούλημα (LN 25.4), and εὐδοκία (LN 25.8), there is a tendency to employ verbs rather than nouns. This is true especially in languages outside the Indo-European family of languages. Wanting, desiring, and wishing are essentially psychological events or states and accordingly are most frequently expressed in languages by verbs.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
s.d: to take pleasure in something in view of its being desirable

s.dp: Communication › Interpret, Mean, Explain
s.d: (an idiom, literally: it wishes to be) something which is to mean or to be understood in a particular manner
s.g: it means; this is to be understood as
s.c: The question in ⟦Acts 2:12|Acts 2:12⟧ does not refer to the immediate meaning of the particular expression but rather to its broader implications, so that the question may very well be rendered as ‘what does this say’ or ‘what does this imply?’

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: that on which a structure is built{N:001}
s.c: In some languages it is possible to describe a typical foundation in ancient times as ‘large stones underneath the walls.’ In other languages, however, this may seem to be quite a meaningless type of expression, since foundations are only made secure by driving stakes deep into the ground. Therefore, it may be best to describe the function of a foundation by ‘what keeps the walls firm’ or ‘how the walls are made not to move’ or ‘what goes beneath the walls.’

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a stone used in the construction of a foundation{N:002}
s.c: Such foundation stones may be described as ‘stones beneath the walls’ or ‘stones beneath the walls to make the walls strong.’

s.dp: Relations › Basis
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θεμέλιος<SDBG:θεμέλιος:000000>}[a] ‘foundation,’ {D:7.41}) the basis for some action or event

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: to lay or construct a foundation
s.g: to lay a foundation; to found something upon

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Trust, Rely
s.d: to provide a firm basis for belief or practice
s.g: to provide a basis for; to provide a foundation for; to cause to be steadfast in

s.dp: Communication › Teach
s.d: pertaining to being taught by God
s.g: taught by God; instructed by God
s.c: In a number of languages the passive expression θεοδίδακτοί ἐστε in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:9|1 Thessalonians 4:9⟧ must be rendered in an active form, for example, ‘for God himself has taught you how you should love one another.’

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Strife, Struggle
s.d: pertaining to fighting against God
s.g: to fight against God; to be against God; to be an enemy of God
s.c: Although the figurative expression ‘fighting against God’ is an unusual and radical figure of speech, it can often be translated more or less literally, but in some languages such an expression is regarded as both impossible and even ludicrous, and therefore one must employ some such expression as ‘to be a constant enemy of God’ or ‘to be always against God.’

s.dp: Communication › Preach, Proclaim
s.d: pertaining to a communication which has been inspired by God
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult to find an appropriate term to render ‘inspired.’ In some instances ‘Scripture inspired by God’ is rendered as ‘Scripture, the writer of which was influenced by God’ or ‘… guided by God.’ It is important, however, to avoid an expression which will mean only ‘dictated by God.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: the one supreme supernatural being as creator and sustainer of the universe
s.c: The componential features of θεός involve a basic, underlying ambivalence. On the one hand, θεός is regarded as unique to the exclusion of all other gods: οὐδεὶς θεὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ‘there is no God but one’ ⟦1 Corinthians 8:4|1 Corinthians 8:4⟧. This is strictly a monotheistic view of θεός. On the other hand, there occur such expressions as εἴπερ εἰσὶν λεγόμενοι θεοί ‘even if there are so-called gods’ (⟦1 Corinthians 8:5|1 Corinthians 8:5⟧), and in the OT the Lord is described as being ‘far above all gods’ (⟦Psalms 97:9|Psalms 97:9⟧), ‘the God of gods’ (⟦Psalms 136:2|Psalms 136:2⟧), and the ‘great King above all gods’ (⟦Psalms 95:3|Psalms 95:3⟧), which is essentially a henotheistic view of θεός. Fundamentally, however, the NT view may be most succinctly reflected in ⟦Galatians 4:8|Galatians 4:8⟧, τοῖς φύσει μὴ οὖσιν θεοῖς ‘those who by nature are not really gods.’ In other words, the gods of the pagans (see LN 12.22) are not to be viewed in the same category as θεός .|A further semantic problem is involved in the use of θεός in reference to Christ. In ⟦John 1:1|John 1:1⟧, the ‘the Word was God,’ the meaning of θεός may be described on the basis that all the componential features of θεός are applied to the referent λόγος, which is in turn identified with ‘Christ.’ This is not to be interpreted as indicating that the two referents are identical (which was, of course, the position of those who maintained the so-called patropassian heresy), but that the distinctive features of θεός are also fully applicable to another referent, namely, the λόγος or Christ; that is to say, it is legitimate to interpret ⟦John 1:1|John 1:1⟧ as ‘the Word was God’ but not as ‘God was the Word.’|Translational equivalents of ‘God’ are of three major types: (1) proper names, (2) descriptive titles, and (3) borrowed terms. There are a number of problems involved in each of these types of translational equivalents.|If translators wish to employ in the biblical text a proper name in the receptor language, it is essential that the characteristics of the referent of such a name be sufficiently close to those which characterize the biblical God, so that the message may not be unduly distorted. In fact, the equivalent should be sufficiently close that ready identification can be made. The essential features of such a receptor language term should include (1) benevolent disposition and behavior, (2) creative and sustaining activity in the world, and (3) supreme power. In most instances it has not been found necessary for such a term to refer to a strictly monotheistic view (that is to say, having an existence which precludes the existence of any other gods), but it is essential that the name apply to a referent who is regarded as supreme over all others.|There may, however, be a number of difficulties involved in the use of an indigenous expression for θεός, since the views concerning such a god may involve such factors as (1) psychological distance (the idea that such a god, though all powerful, is still very remote from mankind) and (2) the necessity for constant propitiation (as though such a god needs to be constantly entreated or sustained by means of gifts in order to make him favorably disposed toward mankind).|In some instances problems have arisen in the use of an indigenous term for God because such a name may be perfectly appropriate in one area in which a language is spoken, but have quite a different meaning or value in another part of the language area. For example, in one area of East Africa the name for ‘God’ in one tribe is the name for the devil in a nearby, closely related tribe.|Descriptive titles for God (which often become essentially names) may focus upon a number of different features or characteristics. In some instances such descriptive titles are traditional for certain receptor languages. In other instances they have been constructed by translators on the basis of indigenous models. The following are illustrative examples of various types of descriptive titles: ‘he who made us,’ ‘the supreme powerful one,’ ‘the one who performs miracles,’ ‘the owner of all,’ ‘he who is sufficient,’ ‘our great father,’ ‘the highest one,’ ‘the great spirit,’ ‘the unending spirit,’ ‘the commanding spirit,’ ‘the great chief,’ ‘the self-existing one,’ and ‘the truly sacred one.’|Some Bible translators have attempted to avoid semantic complications by borrowing a term from a dominant language. In Latin America, for example, many early missionaries borrowed the Spanish term Dios, but in explaining the meaning of Dios as the great and all-powerful creator, they simply provided another name for what people already understood to be the sun. The difficulty with borrowed proper names is that they are essentially zero in meaning, that is to say, they are words with a significant absence of meaning which must be filled in one way or another, and this is usually done merely by equating the meaning of such a zero term with already existing concepts. Hence, rather than avoiding wrong views of God, borrowed terms often perpetuate wrong views indirectly.|There may also be additional complications in the use of a borrowed term, since it may not provide a basis for certain syntactic or morphological modifications. For example, some missionaries have borrowed the term Allah for ‘God,’ but in speaking of ‘gods’ they have attempted to add a plural to the underlying form Allah. In most instances this procedure has resulted in something which is not only conceptually and grammatically impossible, but also highly offensive to receptors.|One special problem involving θεός results from the occurrence of ‘God’ in expressions of possession, for example, ‘my God’ or ‘our God.’ In a number of languages one simply cannot say ‘my God,’ for one cannot ‘possess God.’ Rather, one must say ‘the God whom I worship’ or ‘the God in whom I trust.’ Similarly, it may be impossible to speak of ‘the God of Abraham’ without implying that such a God would only be an idol, that is to say, ‘the God that Abraham personally possessed.’ Under such circumstances it may be necessary to translate ‘the God of Abraham’ as ‘the God in whom Abraham trusted.’|Ideally, one should employ a well known receptor-language term for ‘God’ which would be applicable not only to the one supreme being, but could also refer to the ‘gods of the heathen,’ that is to say, a rendering of θεός should be a generic expression which could be made particular and even exclusive by some such qualifier as ‘the’ or ‘the one’ or ‘the unique.’ Sometimes this can only be done by a qualifier such as ‘the great’ or even ‘the supreme.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: any one of many different supernatural beings regarded as having authority or control over some aspect of the universe or human activity
s.c: Some translators have made a practice of trying to render the meaning of θεός by terms which mean essentially demons or evil spirits, but this is a mistake, for though the gods of the ancient pagans may be regarded as having had no existence at all, nevertheless, the NT does not speak of them as being evil.|In those languages in which there is no contrast between ‘gods’ and ‘spirits,’ that is to say, in instances in which people believe only in indwelling spirits rather than in supernatural beings who have control over natural phenomena, it may be possible to distinguish ‘gods’ by speaking of them as ‘powerful spirits.’ In certain instances, therefore, the equivalent of ‘God’ (LN 12.1) is ‘the all-powerful Spirit.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a female deity
s.c: In some languages it may seem quite strange to attribute female sex to a divine being. However, one can almost always say ‘a woman god’ or ‘a spirit like a woman’ or ‘a spirit thought of as being like a woman.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (a title applied to Jesus, literally: son of God, parallel in semantic structure to phrases consisting of υἱός followed by the genitive of class or kind; compare {D:9.4}) one who has the essential characteristics and nature of God
s.c: Before adopting a translation of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ such as ‘Son of God,’ one must always investigate the extent to which such an expression might already be used in a particular language. For example, in the Tarahumara language of Mexico mankind is divided into two classes: (1) ‘sons of God,’ who are Tarahumaras and (2) ‘sons of the devil,’ all other people. In these circumstances it is necessary in translating υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ to use an expression which will identify ‘the unique Son of God’ or ‘the one who is truly the Son of God.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Religious Practice
s.d: appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
s.c: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Religious Practice
s.d: pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hate, Hateful
s.d: pertaining to hatred for God
s.g: hating God; one who hates God
s.c: It is possible, though unlikely, that θεοστυγής in ⟦Romans 1:30|Romans 1:30⟧ could be interpreted as ‘those whom God hates.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (derivative of {L:θεός<SDBG:θεός:000000>}[a] ‘God,’ {D:12.1}) the nature or state of being God
s.c: The expression ‘divine nature’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘just what God is like’ or ‘how God is’ or ‘what God is.’ In ⟦Romans 1:20|Romans 1:20⟧ ‘deity’ may sometimes be expressed as ‘the fact that he is God’ or ‘… is truly God.’|In ⟦2 Peter 1:4|2 Peter 1:4⟧ ‘to share in the very being of God,’ one may speak of ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to become in a measure like God.’ It is important, of course, to avoid the implication that people can become completely God.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an important Christian to whom the books of Luke and Acts were dedicated

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: causing someone to recover health, often with the implication of having taken care of such a person

s.dp: Household Activities
s.d: the group of servants working in a particular household

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: to cause someone to recover health, often with the implication of having taken care of such a person
s.g: to heal; to cure; to take care of; healing

s.dp: Help, Care For › Serve
s.d: to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
s.g: to serve; to render service; to help; service; help
s.c: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’

s.dp: Help, Care For › Serve
s.d: (derivative of {L:θεραπεύω<SDBG:θεραπεύω:000001>}[b] ‘to serve,’ {D:35.19}) a person who renders service
s.c: In rendering θεράπων, ὑπηρέτης, and διάκονος in the sense of ‘servant,’ it is important to avoid a term which would be too specific, for example, ‘one who serves meals’ or ‘one who works around the house.’ It may, in fact, be necessary to use an expression which means essentially ‘helper.’

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: to cut ripe grain and to gather bundles of such grain together

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: act of cutting ripe grain and gathering bundles of such grain together

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: that which is harvested

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: (derivative of {L:θερίζω<SDBG:θερίζω:000000>} ‘to harvest,’ {D:43.14}) a person who gathers in a crop
s.c: In a number of languages there is no specific term for ‘reapers,’ and therefore it may be necessary in ⟦Matthew 13:30|Matthew 13:30⟧ to say ‘… I will say to those who are working in the fields’ or ‘… who are cutting down the grain.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Hot, Lukewarm, Cold
s.d: to cause oneself to become warm
s.c: In some languages a literal meaning of ‘to warm oneself’ would mean ‘to increase in anger,’ and therefore it may be necessary in a case such as ⟦Mark 14:67|Mark 14:67⟧ to say simply ‘when she saw Peter there near the fire.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Hot, Lukewarm, Cold
s.d: a state of a relatively high degree of heat

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: the warmest period of the year and primarily the season for the growth of vegetation
s.c: In some areas of the Tropics, there are difficulties involved in arriving at a satisfactory term for θέρος. It may not be possible, for example, to use ‘the warm season,’ since that may refer to the end of a dry season just before the rains begin. Normally, therefore, one can equate θέρος with ‘the rainy season,’ but a context such as ⟦Luke 21:30|Luke 21:30⟧ may be difficult, for one would not normally say ‘when you see that the trees are putting out leaves, you know that the rainy season is near,’ for trees normally do not put out the leaves until after the rainy season has begun. It may, therefore, be necessary to render ⟦Luke 21:30|Luke 21:30⟧ as ‘when you see the trees putting out leaves, you know that the time for growth is near’ or ‘… the time for trees to produce fruit.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Θεσσαλονίκη<SDBG:Θεσσαλονίκη:000000>} ‘Thessalonica,’ {D:93.475}) a person who lives in or is a native of Thessalonica

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city of Macedonia

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Jewish insurrectionist

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: to observe something with continuity and attention, often with the implication that what is observed is something unusual
s.g: to observe; to be a spectator of; to look at

s.dp: Understand › Come To Understand
s.d: to come to understand as the result of perception
s.g: to understand; to perceive; to see; to recognize

s.dp: Case › Experiencer
s.d: to experience an event or state, normally in negative expressions indicating what one will not experience

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: (derivative of {L:θεωρέω<SDBG:θεωρέω:000000>}[a] ‘to observe,’ {D:24.14}) an unusual object or event which is observed

s.dp: Artifacts › Containers
s.d: a case or bag about the size and shape of a sword, used to cover and to carry the sword; made of leather, cloth, metal, or even wood; attached to a strap or belt that could be hung over the shoulder or tied around the waist{N:001}
s.c: In this one occurrence of θήκη in the NT, the reference is to a ‘sheath’ for a sword, which may be rendered in some languages as ‘a leather bag for a sword’ or ‘a covering for a sword’ or ‘something in which a sword is carried.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: the activity of a baby feeding at the breast
s.g: to nurse (of a baby); to suck; to feed on
s.c: In a number of languages there are highly specific terms for the manner in which babies nurse, including ‘to suck upon’ or ‘to pull at the breasts.’ There may also be distinctions in terminology depending upon whether the child in question is a helpless infant held in the arms or a small child capable of moving about. See also discussion at LN 23.8.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to cause a baby to feed at the breast
s.c: In many languages entirely distinct terms are employed for the causative and noncausative meanings of ‘to nurse.’ Still additional distinctions may be employed depending upon the age of the child. One term may be used in speaking of helpless infants, while another may be used of small children who are able to walk around, but who still are nursed from time to time.

s.dp: Features of Objects › Male, Female
s.d: the female of any living creature

s.dp: Artifacts › Traps, Snares
s.d: a device used for trapping, especially of animals other than birds

s.dp: Control, Rule › Control, Restrain
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:θήρα<SDBG:θήρα:000000>}[a] ‘trap,’ {D:6.24}) an instrument or means for gaining control, implying an element of surprise
s.g: means of control; way of trapping
s.c: In a number of languages, it is possible to reflect something of the figurative meaning of θήρα by translating this term as a verb, for example, ‘may they be caught and trapped at their feasts’ or ‘may their feasts snare and trap them’ (see LN 6.24).

s.dp: Learn › Learn Something Against Someone
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of term meaning literally ‘to hunt,’ ‘to trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to acquire information about an error or fault, with the purpose of causing harm or trouble
s.g: to trap; to catch off guard; to catch in a mistake
s.c: In a number of languages it is possible to retain the figurative meaning of ‘trap’ or ‘catch,’ but in a number of instances other figures are used, for example, ‘to cause to trip,’ ‘to cause to fall,’ ‘to hear wrong words from his mouth,’ or ‘to use his words against him.’

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Strife, Struggle
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of θηριομαχέω ‘to be forced to fight with wild animals,’ not occurring in the NT) to be in conflict with forceful opposition
s.g: to be in a serious struggle with; to have to contend with
s.c: Some persons have assumed that θηριομαχέω in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:32|1 Corinthians 15:32⟧ is to be understood in a literal sense, but this is very unlikely. One can, however, preserve something of the figurative force of this expression by rendering this question in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:32|1 Corinthians 15:32⟧ as “if I have, as it were, fought ‘wild beasts’ here in Ephesus simply from human motives, what have I gained?” (TEV). By making a metaphor into a simile one can preserve something of the figurative value of the phrase, while at the same time not introducing possible misunderstanding.

s.dp: Animals
s.d: any living creature, not including man

s.dp: Animals
s.d: any four-footed animal, either wild or domesticated
s.c: A high percentage of languages appear to have no generic term to identify all kinds of quadrupeds whether wild or domesticated. Rather, they tend to make quite clear distinctions between wild and domesticated animals, and therefore it may be necessary to indicate both types in those contexts where the reference is to both wild as well as domesticated animals. For example, one may sometimes speak of ‘animals of the grass and animals of the forest’ or ‘animals of the barn and animals of the mountains.’|In ⟦Acts 10:12|Acts 10:12⟧ the reference is primarily to wild animals, since for the most part wild animals would be those designated as unclean. However, swine were also regarded as unclean, and they were domesticated.|In ⟦Revelation 13:1|Revelation 13:1⟧ff two visionary creatures are referred to by the term θηρίον ‘beast.’ Despite their strange symbolic appearance, they would no doubt be included within the potential range of reference of θηρίον .

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θηρίον<SDBG:θηρίον:000001>}[b] ‘(wild) animal,’ {D:4.4}) a bad person, in the sense of being both harmful and dangerous
s.g: bad person; wicked person; evil beast
s.c: The translation of θηρίον as merely ‘wild animal’ may be seriously misunderstood in some languages, since speaking of a person as ‘a wild animal’ might be a compliment based upon the idea of strength and courage. It may, therefore, be necessary to use some such expression as ‘dangerous animal’ or ‘harmful wild animal.’

s.dp: Value › Valuable, Lacking in Value
s.d: (derivative of {L:θησαυρός<SDBG:θησαυρός:000002>}[c] ‘treasure,’ {D:65.10}) to keep safe that which is of great value
s.g: to treasure up; to keep safe

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θησαυρίζω<SDBG:θησαυρίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to treasure up,’ {D:65.11}) to cause something of a more extensive nature to happen in the future
s.g: to make even greater; to cause to happen more intensely or more extensively

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room for the storage of valuables
s.c: ταμεῖον and θησαυρός may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In ⟦Matthew 12:35|Matthew 12:35⟧ θησαυρός is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

s.dp: Artifacts › Containers
s.d: a box in which money was kept
s.c: A ‘treasure box’ may be referred to as ‘a box with valuable objects’ or ‘a box with objects costing a great deal of money.’

s.dp: Value › Valuable, Lacking in Value
s.d: that which is of exceptional value and kept safe

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Touch, Feel
s.d: to come in contact with
s.c: It is also possible in ⟦Hebrews 11:28|Hebrews 11:28⟧ that θιγγάνω is to be understood in the sense of ‘to kill’ (see LN 20.75).

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Kill
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θιγγάνω<SDBG:θιγγάνω:000000>}[a] ‘to touch,’ {D:24.74}) to cause the death of someone, perhaps suggesting some supernatural or mysterious means
s.g: to kill; to slay; to cause the death of

s.dp: Physical Impact › Press
s.d: to crowd in hard against{N:001}
s.g: to press against; to crowd against

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Cause Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to cause someone to suffer trouble or hardship
s.g: to cause trouble to; to persecute; to cause to suffer hardship

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Experience Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to suffer hardship
s.g: to suffer hardship; to be troubled

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: trouble involving direct suffering
s.c: For a number of languages ‘trouble and suffering’ may be expressed as ‘that which causes pain.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: the process of dying
s.c: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: pertaining to being liable to death (that which will eventually die)
s.c: The phrase ‘mortal bodies’ (⟦Romans 6:12|Romans 6:12⟧) may be rendered as ‘bodies which will die.’

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Riot
s.d: to cause people to riot against
s.g: to stir up against; to start a riot; to cause an uproar

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: to be emotionally upset by a concern or anxiety
s.g: to be troubled; to be distressed; to be upset
s.c: It is also possible to interpret θορυβέομαι in ⟦Acts 20:10|Acts 20:10⟧ as referring to the evident commotion caused by the fall of Eutychus from a window. Accordingly, one may translate as ‘stop this commotion; he is still alive.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Sound
s.d: noise or clamor marked by confusion
s.c: In some languages it may be legitimate to translate θόρυβος in ⟦Acts 21:34|Acts 21:34⟧ as ‘so much noise from so many people shouting’ or ‘because so many people were shouting different things.’

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Riot
s.d: disorderly behavior of people in violent opposition to authority

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Cause Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to cause serious trouble to, with the implication of dire consequences and probably a weakened state
s.g: to cause severe hardship; to oppress; to overwhelm

s.dp: Animals
s.d: domesticated four-footed animals, primarily livestock
s.c: τὰ θρέμματα in ⟦John 4:12|John 4:12⟧ would include cattle (bulls, cows, oxen), sheep, goats, donkeys, and possibly camels. It is difficult, however, to obtain in certain languages an expression which is sufficiently generic as to include all such domesticated animals. Sometimes, however, one can use a phrase such as ‘animals that people take care of’ or ‘animals that are herded’ or even ‘animals that are owned.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: to weep or cry, especially in mourning for the dead{N:001}
s.c: For another interpretation of θρηνέω in ⟦Luke 23:27|Luke 23:27⟧, see LN 52.2.|Mourning and wailing for the dead are frequently expressed by a term very different from expressions employed in referring to events not involving death.

s.dp: Communication › Sing, Lament
s.d: to sing or chant expressions of mourning
s.g: to sing funeral songs; to chant a dirge

s.dp: Funerals and Burial
s.d: to wail and lament for the dead, implying a ritualized form of mourning at funerals{N:002}
s.c: For another interpretation of θρηνέω in ⟦Luke 23:27|Luke 23:27⟧, see LN 25.141.

s.dp: Religious Activities › Religious Practice
s.d: appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
s.c: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Religious Practice
s.d: pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Conquer
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of θριαμβεύω ‘to lead prisoners of war in a victory procession,’ not occurring in the NT) to demonstrate one’s successful conquest of opposition
s.g: to triumph over; to be completely victorious over
s.c: Since the leading of prisoners of war in a victory procession is at the present time a relatively rare cultural phenomenon, it may be impossible to employ such a literal rendering of θριαμβεύω. One may, however, wish to employ a marginal note to indicate the background meaning of θριαμβεύω in this context.

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Conquer
s.d: to cause someone to completely triumph over
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of triumphing without indicating the goal of such an event, but in ⟦2 Corinthians 2:14|2 Corinthians 2:14⟧ there is no specified object over which triumph occurs. It is possible to introduce Satan as the one over whom the believer is victorious (see ⟦2 Corinthians 2:11|2 Corinthians 2:11⟧). However, it is also possible to understand θριαμβεύω in ⟦2 Corinthians 2:14|2 Corinthians 2:14⟧ as being essentially similar in meaning to θριαμβεύω (LN 39.59) and thus to translate ⟦2 Corinthians 2:14|2 Corinthians 2:14⟧ as ‘for in union with Christ we are always led by God as prisoners in Christ’s victorious procession.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: hair, either of a person or of an animal
s.c: In a number of languages important distinctions are made between the hair of animals and the hair of humans. Further distinctions may also be made between the hair of the head, the hair of the beard, and general body hair. In certain instances special terms are also used for pubic hair.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: to be in a state of fear associated with surprise
s.c: For the reference of διὰ πνεύματος in ⟦2 Thessalonians 2:2|2 Thessalonians 2:2⟧, see commentaries.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: a small amount of blood in coagulated form
s.g: clot of blood; drop of blood

s.dp: Artifacts › Furniture
s.d: a relatively large and elaborate seat upon which a ruler sits on official occasions
s.c: In some languages ‘throne’ is rendered as ‘the seat of judging’ or ‘the seat of decision-making for a ruler.’

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θρόνος<SDBG:θρόνος:000000>}[a] ‘throne,’ {D:6.112}) a ruling power, with the implication of royal status
s.c: Most scholars understand θρόνος in ⟦Colossians 1:16|Colossians 1:16⟧ as meaning a supernatural power, whether angelic or demonic (see LN 12.44), but it is possible that θρόνοι in ⟦Colossians 1:16|Colossians 1:16⟧ means human rulers.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
s.g: power; authority; lordship; ruler; wicked force
s.c: See also LN 37.52, LN 37.70, and LN 37.73.

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: position of power and authority to rule
s.c: There are serious complications in attempting to translate θρόνος in ⟦Luke 1:32|Luke 1:32⟧ literally as ‘throne,’ since this might refer specifically to the seat on which David earlier sat. It may in fact be necessary to translate this expression in ⟦Luke 1:32|Luke 1:32⟧ as ‘the Lord God will cause him to rule in the way in which his ancestor David ruled.’

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: the place from which authority or rule is exercised
s.g: place of authority; place of ruling; throne
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 4:16|Hebrews 4:16⟧ the phrase τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος is clearly a reference to God, and therefore in a number of languages it may be necessary to translate ‘let us therefore with boldness approach God, who shows grace.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Lydia

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: immediate female offspring
s.c: A literal rendering of ⟦Matthew 10:37|Matthew 10:37⟧, namely, ‘whoever loves his son or daughter more than me,’ may be misleading, since in some languages it could refer to only one particular son or daughter. A more indefinite expression may therefore be preferable, namely, ‘any one of his sons or daughters.’

s.dp: People › Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θυγάτηρ<SDBG:θυγάτηρ:000000>}[a] ‘daughter,’ {D:10.46}) a woman for whom there is some affectionate concern
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate θυγάτηρ literally as ‘daughter,’ since this would imply that Jesus was acknowledging that the woman was in fact his own daughter. An obvious adjustment must be made in such instances, and therefore one may use such expressions as lady or my dear woman.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (an extended meaning of {L:θυγάτηρ<SDBG:θυγάτηρ:000000>}[a] ‘daughter,’ {D:10.46}) a nonimmediate female descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations)
s.c: See discussion at υἱός LN 10.30 and its footnote.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θυγάτηρ<SDBG:θυγάτηρ:000000>}[a] ‘daughter,’ {D:10.46}) a female inhabitant of a place

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: (an idiom, literally: daughter of Zion) the inhabitants of Jerusalem
s.g: people of Zion; people of Jerusalem

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (a diminutive derivative of {L:θυγάτηρ<SDBG:θυγάτηρ:000000>}[a] daughter, {D:10.46}, with possible emphasis upon young age and probable implication of affection)
s.c: In ⟦Mark 5:23|Mark 5:23⟧ the text indicates specifically that the daughter was twelve years of age, and it may very well be that in ⟦Mark 7:25|Mark 7:25⟧ (the only other passage in which θυγάτριον occurs in the NT) the daughter may have been of approximately the same age. In languages in which some indication of relative age is obligatory, one could employ a term identifying a girl about the age of puberty.

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Wind
s.d: sudden and violent gusts of winds, often from varied directions{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages a strong wind which causes the waves or a storm on water must be referred to by a special term. Compare, for example, the English term squall; this would mean a wind of relatively short duration but sufficiently intense so as to create relatively high waves.

s.dp: Plants › Wood and Wood Products
s.d: pertaining to being made or consisting of citron wood (that is, from a citron tree, a coniferous tree related to cypresses, pines, and cedars; up to 9 m high; scaly leaves, reddish brown bark, sweet-smelling wood)
s.c: The citron tree belongs to the citrus family of plants, and it produces a pale yellow fruit somewhat larger than a lemon, the rind of which is often candied. In ⟦Revelation 18:12|Revelation 18:12⟧, however, the focus is upon the fine quality of the wood, and since citron trees are not known in many parts of the world, it may be useful to translate πᾶν ξύλον θύϊνον simply as ‘all kinds of valuable wood.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Perfumes and Incense
s.d: any aromatic substance (usually a resin) burned for its pleasing aroma
s.c: Since some form of incense is almost universal, there is normally no difficulty involved in finding some term to designate ‘incense.’ However, it is always possible to employ a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘a substance which gives off a sweet-smelling smoke’ or ‘… a good-smelling smoke.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Offering, Sacrifice
s.d: to burn aromatic substances as an offering to God
s.g: to offer incense; to burn incense; incense offering

s.dp: Artifacts › Furniture
s.d: a relatively small altar used for burning incense; made of wood
s.c: θυμιατήριον may be rendered in some languages as ‘place where incense is burned in worship of God.’ One must avoid a rendering which would imply that the altar was made of incense.

s.dp: Religious Activities › Offering, Sacrifice
s.d: to burn aromatic substances as an offering to God
s.g: to offer incense; to burn incense; incense offering

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: to be extremely angry, with the implication of violence
s.g: to be violently angry; to be furious
s.c: For another interpretation of θυμομαχέω in ⟦Acts 12:20|Acts 12:20⟧, see LN 33.453.

s.dp: Communication › Argue, Quarrel
s.d: to engage in an angry quarrel with someone
s.g: to be angry and quarrel; to quarrel angrily
s.c: For another interpretation of θυμομαχέω in ⟦Acts 12:20|Acts 12:20⟧, see LN 88.180.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: a state of intense anger, with the implication of passionate outbursts
s.c: In a number of contexts θυμός is combined with ὀργή (LN 88.173) in such a manner that the meaning of one simply heightens the intensity or significance of the other, as in ⟦Romans 2:8|Romans 2:8⟧, τοῖς δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πειθομένοις δὲ τῇ ἀδικίᾳὀργὴ καὶ θυμός ‘and to those who out of jealousy reject the truth and adhere to evil, there will be fury and anger.’ But in a number of languages it is necessary to specify who experiences such anger or fury, and therefore it may be necessary to translate ‘God will be furious and angry against them.’ The fury and anger of God is generally interpreted in terms of ‘divine retribution and punishment.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire Strongly
s.d: an intense, passionate desire of an overwhelming and possibly destructive character

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: (derivative of {L:θυμός<SDBG:θυμός:000000>}[a] ‘anger,’ {D:88.178}) to be extremely angry, even to the point of being in a rage
s.c: In some instances it may be possible to speak of ‘being extremely angry’ as ‘to be so angry as not to be able to think.’

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: the door to a house or building (often occurring in plural form and designating double doors or gates)

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: the entranceway into a building or structure
s.c: In ⟦John 10:9|John 10:9⟧ θύρα is used figuratively to refer to Jesus as the means of access to salvation: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα δἰ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθω σωθήσεται ‘I am the door; whoever comes in by me will be saved.’ In ⟦John 10:9|John 10:9⟧ the emphasis is upon the door as a passageway and not as an object closing off an entrance. Literal translations of ‘I am the door’ may often lead to misinterpretation, since the term used for ‘door’ is likely to refer to a literal door rather than to the entranceway, thus suggesting that Jesus Christ functions primarily to prevent passage rather than making entrance possible.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time subsequent to another point of time and indicating imminence, that is to say, the subsequent event is regarded as almost begun

s.dp: Artifacts › Weapons and Armor
s.d: a long, oblong shield; used to protect the entire body in battle; made of wood, metal, leather stretched over wood, or plaited strips of wood or reeds
s.c: In some languages ‘shield’ is described as ‘protection one carries when one fights’ or ‘protection carried to prevent blows from the enemy.’ The phrase ἀναλαβόντες τὸν θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως may thus be rendered as ‘take hold of faith as a protection against the enemy’ or ‘regard your faith as a protection to prevent the attacks of the enemy.’

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: an opening in a wall for the entrance of light and air and for the purpose of seeing in or out

s.dp: Household Activities
s.d: one who guards the door giving access to a house or building

s.dp: Religious Activities › Offering, Sacrifice
s.d: that which is offered as a sacrifice

s.dp: Artifacts › Furniture
s.d: any type of altar or object where gifts may be placed and ritual observances carried out in honor of supernatural beings (in the NT θυσιαστήριον is employed to refer to a number of different types of altars; including the altar for burnt offerings in the Temple; the altar of incense; the altar which Abraham built; and the heavenly altar mentioned in the book of Revelation)
s.c: A descriptive equivalent of ‘altar’ occurs in some languages as ‘a place where offerings are made to God’ or ‘a place where gifts are given to God.’ In some contexts it may be necessary to add phrases such as ‘where sacrifices are burned to God’ or ‘where incense is burned to honor God.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Offering, Sacrifice
s.d: to slaughter an animal in a ritual manner as a sacrifice to deity
s.g: to sacrifice; to make a sacrifice

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Kill
s.d: to slaughter, either animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the twelve apostles; see also {D:93.95}

s.dp: Artifacts › Weapons and Armor
s.d: a piece of armor covering the chest to protect it against blows and arrows

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the portion of the upper trunk covered by the breastplate
s.c: Note, however, that in ⟦Revelation 9:9|Revelation 9:9⟧ it is possible to understand the first occurrence of θώραξ in the sense of ‘breastplate,’ the meaning which it normally has in other biblical contexts (for example, ⟦Ephesians 6:14|Ephesians 6:14⟧ and ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:8|1 Thessalonians 5:8⟧). The passage could then be translated as ‘their breastplates were iron breastplates’ (see LN 6.39).

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a synagogue official

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the patriarch Jacob, a son of Isaac

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of {L:Ἰωσήφ<SDBG:Ἰωσήφ:000001>}[b] in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the twelve apostles and the son of Zebedee and brother of John

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a brother of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the son of Alphaeus and one of the twelve apostles
s.c: Some scholars consider Ἰάκωβος and Ἰάκωβος to be the same person.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the son of {L:Mary<SDBG:Μαρία:000003>}[d] and called ‘the younger’ in {S:04101504000034}
s.c: Some scholars consider Ἰάκωβος and Ἰάκωβος to be the same person.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of Judas, one of the twelve apostles

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a tax collector called ‘James’ rather than ‘Levi’ ({S:04100201400008}, apparatus)

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἰάομαι<SDBG:ἰάομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to cause to be well again, to heal,’ {D:23.136}) the capacity to cause someone to become healed or cured
s.g: the power to heal; the capacity to heal
s.c: In some languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘giving the power to heal.’ A more natural form of expression is ‘cause to be able to heal.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jannes opposed Moses before Pharaoh

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jambres opposed Moses before Pharaoh

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: to cause someone to become well again after having been sick{N:001}
s.g: to heal; to cure; to make well; healing
s.c: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἰάομαι<SDBG:ἰάομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to heal,’ {D:23.136}) to cause something to change to an earlier, correct, or appropriate state

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of Enoch in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
s.g: to heal; to cure; to make well; healing
s.c: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: jasper; probably green in color (see {D:2.29})

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the host of Paul and Silas in Thessalonica

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person who sends greetings in {S:04501602100020}

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: one who causes someone to be healed

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: pertaining to being the exclusive property of someone{N:001}

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Distinctive, Unique
s.d: pertaining to that which is peculiar or distinctive to some entity

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a reference to each one individually

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: persons who in some sense belong to a so-called reference person

s.dp: Know › Able To Be Known
s.d: (an idiom, literally: according to that which is private) pertaining to what occurs in a private context or setting, in the sense of not being made known publicly

s.dp: Learn
s.d: a person who has not acquired systemic information or expertise in some field of knowledge or activity
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 14:16|1 Corinthians 14:16⟧ ἰδιώτης is used to refer to a class of persons who were neither unbelievers nor fully instructed Christians, but who were inquirers or catechumens. In such a context, ἰδιώτης may be rendered as ‘ordinary, uninitiated’ (ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς ἐν πνεύματι, ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμήν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ ‘when you give thanks to God in spirit only, how can an ordinary, uninitiated person taking part in the meeting say “Amen” to your prayer of thanksgiving’).
